11.text: still more solid, the central poles and some of the most important joints of

12.text: the frame are strengthened by means of heavy stones tied to them with ropes,

13.text: or by loaded sledges, which are pushed from inside against the skin cover,

14.text: the lower end of which is secured under the runners. The sledges are con-

15.text: nected with the upper part of the frame by taut cords. Fastened with thongs

16.text: and secured with stones and sledges, the Chukchee tent is able to withstand

17.text: the fiercest wind-storms of the open tundra. I had occasion, however, to

18.text: witness a snowstorm which very quickly battered the frame, and almost caused

19.text: the collapse of the tent. The deep masses of snow which drifted against

20.text: one side of the tent gradually bent the poles out of shape.

23.text: fastened with cords which have been sewed to its ends. A circular opening

24.text: is left at the top for purposes of ventilation. The strongest of these cords

25.text: are drawn across the tent inside, and fastened to the bottoms of the central

26.text: poles or to heavy sledges. An entrance is left between the two halves of

27.text: the cover, so that one end of the flap may be turned aside and then fall

28.text: back by its own weight. The cover is made of skins of full-grown reindeer,

29.text: which have previously done service as covers of the inner room. The thick

30.text: hair of these, however, is closely clipped off to make them lighter. In front,

31.text: a piece of walrus-gut or of well-scraped thin reindeer-skin is sometimes inserted

32.text: to admit light. The Chukchee generally have two tent-covers in use at the

33.text: same time, — one for winter, made of new skins, in which every small hole

34.text: is carefully patched (Plate XII, Fig. 2); and an old one for the summer. In

36.text: The Chukchee pick out for camps flat places without too much snow.

37.text: After the places for the tents have been designated, the women scrape off

38.text: the snow with adze-shaped scrapers of antler or of bone (Fig. 93). They pull

39.text: up all the small shrubs, and then fill in the holes with loose earth or snow.
